paper.abstract: Abstract We develop a quantitative approximation framework for diffusion distillation, viewing few-step sampling as error propagation under compositions of learned flow maps. Focusing on trajectory distillation for the probability-flow ODE, we show that local approximation errors can be strongly amplified in low-noise multimodal regimes, where the underlying dynamics become stiff. In an analytically tractable Gaussian-mixture Ornstein–Uhlenbeck setting, we separate two core difficulties: approximating the time-dependent score field and controlling the dynamical amplification governed by the time-integrated Jacobian bound of the probability-flow ODE. On the approximation side, we prove constructive L p ​ ( p t ) L^{p}(p_{t}) guarantees showing that ReLU–ReQU networks approximate the Gaussian-mixture score uniformly over time, with depth and width scaling polylogarithmically in the target accuracy and explicitly with the mixture geometry. On the stability side, we derive an explicit bound L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) for the spatial Lipschitz constant of the probability-flow velocity and convert it into a flow map stability estimate governed by ∫ s t L ⁡ ( u ) ​ 𝑑 u \int_{s}^{t}L(u)\,du , making late-time amplification in stiff regimes computable. Building on these estimates, we prove that deep residual compositions efficiently approximate the long-horizon transport, with global error controlled by the stability amplification factor, and identify a Lipschitz-mismatch regime in which one-step distillation is structurally unfavorable. The resulting theory yields a stability-balanced non-uniform time grid obtained by uniform partitioning in the cumulative stability coordinate. Experiments support the prediction and reduce end-to-end relative MSE by up to 51.9 % 51.9\% with 8 8 segments compared with uniform grids.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
This paper studies diffusion distillation with deep neural networks from the perspective of approximation theory. The goal is to compress a long-horizon generative transport into a small number of learned maps while preserving sample quality. Diffusion models have become a leading paradigm for generative modeling, enabling high-fidelity synthesis across modalities and finding increasing use in scientific and engineering applications [ 14 , 23 , 42 ] . In their continuous-time formulation [ 42 ] , a forward stochastic process transports a complex data distribution to a simple Gaussian prior and induces a family of marginals { p t } t ∈ [ 0 , T ] \{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} . Generation then amounts to reversing this transport through either the reverse-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) or the deterministic probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE), which share the same marginal laws. This formulation reduces learning to estimating the score ∇ 𝒙 ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝒙 )

Thus, generation quality depends both on the accuracy of the learned vector field and on the way approximation errors propagate along the long-horizon flow. The need for long-horizon numerical integration makes inference with diffusion models expensive, and has motivated substantial work on accelerating sampling. Early approaches mainly focused on fast solvers that reuse a pretrained model and reduce the number of function evaluations through improved discretizations or higher-order ODE schemes, including DDIM [ 40 ] , DPM-Solver [ 31 ] , UniPC [ 55 ] , and EDM-style sampling designs [ 25 ] . These methods can substantially reduce computation, but they still require multiple model evaluations and their sample quality may degrade when the step budget becomes very small. More recently, distillation has become a widely used alternative for accelerating diffusion sampling. In particular, trajectory distillation compresses a pretrained sampler by learning a small number of student updates that imitate the teacher’s multistep reverse-time denoising trajectory, as in progressive distillation [ 36 ] , consistency models [ 41 ] , and data-free variants such as BOOT [ 19 ] . Other distillation strategies, including distribution matching [ 58 , 52 , 51 ] and adversarial distillation [ 37 ] , instead emphasize global distributional alignment or perceptual objectives and need not reproduce the teacher dynamics. In parallel, another line of work trains generic one-step or few-step generators from scratch, such as mean-flow models [ 18 ] and shortcut diffusion models [ 13 ] . We focus on trajectory distillation because it retains the teacher as a reference transport and turns few-step sampling into an error-propagation problem: local discrepancies can be amplified by the Grönwall factor associated with the Jacobian of the reference flow, especially in low-noise, multimodal regimes where the dynamics become stiff. Despite rapid empirical progress, the theoretical understanding of diffusion distillation remains limited. In particular, it is still unclear how to quantify the error incurred when a teacher’s long-horizon transport is replaced by only a small number of learned maps, and how these errors accumulate under composition. A theoretical viewpoint is therefore useful for clarifying the limitations of few-step students and for guiding principled algorithm and time-grid design. This viewpoint yields a segment-wise measure of distillation difficulty and leads to a non-uniform time discretization that balances this difficulty over the full horizon. To keep the analysis tractable without removing the mechanism responsible for multimodal stiffness, we specialize to an isotropic Gaussian mixture model (GMM) initialization evolved by an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) forward process. The same closed-form structure separates two effects. At each fixed time, score approximation remains a nontrivial neural approximation problem whose complexity depends on the mixture geometry. Across time, local approximation errors are propagated by the flow and may accumulate into large trajectory errors when the integrated stability bound is large. This separation underlies the subsequent theory and motivates the stability-balanced discretization strategy used in multistage distillation.

sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 3 introduces the GMM–OU setting and derives closed-form formulas for the score, the Hessian, and the stability bound of the probability-flow ODE. Section 4 studies score approximation by ReLU–ReQU networks and quantifies how the required network complexity depends on the mixture parameters and the target accuracy. Section 5 uses the Jacobian-based stability bound to identify a Lipschitz-mismatch obstruction for one-step distillation, proves an efficient approximation result for finite-time flow maps by deep residual compositions, and develops a stability-balanced time discretization rule. Section 6 provides empirical validation, and the appendices contain proofs and supporting technical results.

sections.heading: Theoretical studies of diffusion models.
sections.text: One line of theory studies diffusion models under general distributional assumptions and establishes approximation, statistical, and computational guarantees. Approximation results show that deep networks can approximate score functions while avoiding the curse of dimensionality under suitable structural assumptions [ 9 , 35 , 43 , 48 ] . Statistical analyses further show that the sample complexity can depend on the intrinsic dimension of the data distribution rather than the ambient dimension [ 4 , 5 , 26 ] . Other works connect score matching with neural tangent kernels to obtain generalization bounds [ 21 ] , or provide evaluation-complexity guarantees for higher-order training-free sampling schemes [ 28 ] . A second line of work studies diffusion models in analytically tractable regimes, with Gaussian mixtures serving as a canonical model class for deriving sharper guarantees. In this setting, prior work has studied parameter identifiability and recovery [ 17 , 38 ] , solver robustness [ 24 , 30 , 20 ] , and mechanisms for exact inversion or polynomial approximation [ 53 , 47 ] . The same mixture framework has also been used to characterize distributional dynamics and sampling limits, including critical windows for feature emergence [ 29 ] , sample-complexity estimates [ 8 ] , and discretization bounds [ 46 ] . It has further enabled analyses of training objectives, including limitations of guidance [ 7 ] , memorization trade-offs [ 3 , 15 , 57 ] , and velocity field matching [ 45 ] . These works provide important insights into diffusion dynamics, but they do not quantify the composition error that arises when a continuous-time flow is replaced by a short sequence of learned maps, which is the central operation in trajectory distillation. Our work belongs to this analytic line, but focuses on the missing composition mechanism. We formulate distillation as flow map approximation under composition and derive bounds that separate segment-level approximation error from dynamical amplification. To quantify this amplification, we specialize to an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process initialized from a Gaussian mixture. This setting remains nontrivial: although the forward dynamics are linear, the multimodal initialization induces a nonlinear score field in which posterior mixture weights can change rapidly, capturing the stiffness and perturbation sensitivity of the probability flow in low-noise regimes. By deriving closed-form expressions for the score and its Jacobian, we obtain computable bounds on the time-dependent Jacobian of the probability-flow ODE. This analysis explains why few-step students may fail in stiff multimodal regimes even when the score is accurately approximated at fixed times, and it motivates stability-balanced discretization rules that refine the time grid where error amplification is strongest.

sections.heading: Stability, stiffness, and Lipschitz constraints.
sections.text: A related line of work studies stability and smoothness properties of diffusion dynamics, since stiff vector fields and large Lipschitz constants can hinder both training and sampling [ 54 , 50 ] . This regularity viewpoint has led to end-time scaling and Lipschitz-guided schedule design for mitigating singular behavior and mode collapse near the origin [ 50 , 6 ] . Within Gaussian mixture settings, researchers have also derived component-independent Lipschitz bounds and designed moment-matching solvers with rigorous sampling stability guarantees [ 30 , 20 ] . Our theory connects this stability viewpoint directly to multistage distillation. We show that the difficulty of a flow segment is determined not only by fixed-time score approximation, but also by the stiffness of the induced flow and its sensitivity to perturbations. This reveals regimes in which the score field is comparatively easy to approximate while the composed transport remains highly unstable. Based on the resulting time-dependent Jacobian bound, we derive a stability-balanced discretization rule that refines the time grid where amplification is large, thereby reducing error accumulation in stiff regimes.

sections.heading: 3 Theoretical Setup

Specifically, we consider a VP diffusion whose marginals { p t } t ∈ [ 0 , T ] \{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} are generated by an OU process [ 42 ] , initialized from an isotropic GMM. sections.heading: 4 Approximation Theory for Score Learning
sections.text: This section studies the network complexity of approximating score functions. For each fixed time t t , the target map is 𝒙 ↦ ∇ 𝒙 ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝒙 ) \bm{x}\mapsto\nabla_{\bm{x}}\log p_{t}(\bm{x}) , and we ask how large a neural network must be to approximate this map to a prescribed accuracy. We work with a ReLU–ReQU hypothesis class ℱ \mathcal{F} , which is convenient for implementing the algebraic operations and normalized exponential weights appearing in the Gaussian-mixture score. The main result shows that, in the GMM–OU setting introduced in Section 3 , the score can be approximated uniformly over t ∈ [ 0 , T ] t\in[0,T] with depth and width depending on the target accuracy ε \varepsilon only through polylogarithmic factors.

sections.heading: 5 Flow Approximation and Stability-Balanced Distillation
sections.text: In Section 4 , we established an approximation result for score learning in the GMM–OU setting. For any fixed t t , within a suitable ReLU–ReQU hypothesis class, one can achieve high-accuracy approximation in L p ​ ( p t ) L^{p}(p_{t}) with complexity on the order of polylog ⁡ ( ε − 1 ) \mathrm{polylog}(\varepsilon^{-1}) . Consequently, the main bottleneck for distillation is often not whether one can fit 𝒗 ⁡ ( ⋅ , t ) \bm{v}(\cdot,t) accurately enough at each time, but rather how this error is amplified by the flow map induced by long-time integration. In this section, we quantify such amplification through a computable bound on the time-dependent Jacobian of the probability-flow ODE, use the resulting stability factor to prove an efficient approximation result for finite-time flow maps by deep residual compositions, and then derive practical principles for choosing a time grid.

For any increasing partition 0 = τ 0 < ⋯ < τ n = T 0=\tau_{0}<\cdots<\tau_{n}=T , the exact flow satisfies the semigroup decomposition Φ 0 ← T = Φ τ 0 ← τ 1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ Φ τ n − 1 ← τ n . \Phi_{0\leftarrow T}=\Phi_{\tau_{0}\leftarrow\tau_{1}}\circ\cdots\circ\Phi_{\tau_{n-1}\leftarrow\tau_{n}}. Thus, depth is not only a way to enlarge a generic function class; here it is used to distribute the long-horizon dynamics over shorter intervals with skip connections. This observation motivates the stability-balanced discretization rule in Subsection 5.3 , where the time horizon is partitioned so that different flow segments have comparable integrated stability scales.

sections.heading: 6.2 Demonstrating flow stiffness via Lipschitz mismatch
sections.text: In this subsection, we empirically validate the stiffness mechanism predicted by Theorem 2 , namely that accurate approximation of the backward probability-flow map requires a student class with sufficient Lipschitz budget, and that this requirement becomes more stringent as the score field sharpens. We fix d = 64 d=64 , K = 20 K=20 , uniform weights π k = 1 / K \pi_{k}=1/K , and an OU decay m t = exp ⁡ ( − β ​ t ) m_{t}=\exp(-\beta t) with β = 5 \beta=5 and T = 1 T=1 . sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This work offers a principled approximation framework for distilling diffusion models and provides both theoretical guarantees and practical algorithms. We proved that, in the isotropic GMM–OU setting, the score of the target distribution can be approximated by neural networks whose size grows only polylogarithmically with the desired accuracy. We introduced a stability profile to quantify how errors amplify over time and showed that, in low‑noise multimodal regimes, the exponential stability factor can exceed the Lipschitz budget of standard network classes. To mitigate this mismatch, we proposed a residual architecture that composes many short‑interval flow approximations and proved an error bound that scales with the stability exponent and the number of blocks. We further devised a stability‑balanced discretization that allocates smaller step sizes in stiff regimes and empirically validated that it substantially reduces end‑to‑end error compared with uniform grids. Together, these results clarify the fundamental limits of trajectory distillation and suggest practical strategies for designing students and time grids. Future work may extend the analysis to more general data distributions, investigate learnability and optimization dynamics, and explore other architectures such as transformers for stability‑aware distillation.

Focusing on trajectory distillation for the probability-flow ODE, we show that local approximation errors can be strongly amplified in low-noise multimodal regimes, where the underlying dynamics become stiff. In an analytically tractable Gaussian-mixture Ornstein–Uhlenbeck setting, we separate two core difficulties: approximating the time-dependent score field and controlling the dynamical amplification governed by the time-integrated Jacobian bound of the probability-flow ODE. On the approximation side, we prove constructive L p ​ ( p t ) L^{p}(p_{t}) guarantees showing that ReLU–ReQU networks approximate the Gaussian-mixture score uniformly over time, with depth and width scaling polylogarithmically in the target accuracy and explicitly with the mixture geometry. On the stability side, we derive an explicit bound L ⁡ ( t ) L(t) for the spatial Lipschitz constant of the probability-flow velocity and convert it into a flow map stability estimate governed by ∫ s t L ⁡ ( u ) ​ 𝑑 u \int_{s}^{t}L(u)\,du , making late-time amplification in stiff regimes computable. Building on these estimates, we prove that deep residual compositions efficiently approximate the long-horizon transport, with global error controlled by the stability amplification factor, and identify a Lipschitz-mismatch regime in which one-step distillation is structurally unfavorable. The resulting theory yields a stability-balanced non-uniform time grid obtained by uniform partitioning in the cumulative stability coordinate. Experiments support the prediction and reduce end-to-end relative MSE by up to 51.9 % 51.9\% with 8 8 segments compared with uniform grids. 1 Introduction This paper studies diffusion distillation with deep neural networks from the perspective of approximation theory. The goal is to compress a long-horizon generative transport into a small number of learned maps while preserving sample quality. Diffusion models have become a leading paradigm for generative modeling, enabling high-fidelity synthesis across modalities and finding increasing use in scientific and engineering applications [ 14 , 23 , 42 ] . In their continuous-time formulation [ 42 ] , a forward stochastic process transports a complex data distribution to a simple Gaussian prior and induces a family of marginals { p t } t ∈ [ 0 , T ] \{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} . Generation then amounts to reversing this transport through either the reverse-time stochastic differential equation (SDE) or the deterministic probability flow ordinary differential equation (ODE), which share the same marginal laws. This formulation reduces learning to estimating the score ∇ 𝒙 ​ log ​ p t ​ ( 𝒙 )

Thus, generation quality depends both on the accuracy of the learned vector field and on the way approximation errors propagate along the long-horizon flow. The need for long-horizon numerical integration makes inference with diffusion models expensive, and has motivated substantial work on accelerating sampling. Early approaches mainly focused on fast solvers that reuse a pretrained model and reduce the number of function evaluations through improved discretizations or higher-order ODE schemes, including DDIM [ 40 ] , DPM-Solver [ 31 ] , UniPC [ 55 ] , and EDM-style sampling designs [ 25 ] . These methods can substantially reduce computation, but they still require multiple model evaluations and their sample quality may degrade when the step budget becomes very small. More recently, distillation has become a widely used alternative for accelerating diffusion sampling. In particular, trajectory distillation compresses a pretrained sampler by learning a small number of student updates that imitate the teacher’s multistep reverse-time denoising trajectory, as in progressive distillation [ 36 ] , consistency models [ 41 ] , and data-free variants such as BOOT [ 19 ] . Other distillation strategies, including distribution matching [ 58 , 52 , 51 ] and adversarial distillation [ 37 ] , instead emphasize global distributional alignment or perceptual objectives and need not reproduce the teacher dynamics. In parallel, another line of work trains generic one-step or few-step generators from scratch, such as mean-flow models [ 18 ] and shortcut diffusion models [ 13 ] . We focus on trajectory distillation because it retains the teacher as a reference transport and turns few-step sampling into an error-propagation problem: local discrepancies can be amplified by the Grönwall factor associated with the Jacobian of the reference flow, especially in low-noise, multimodal regimes where the dynamics become stiff. Despite rapid empirical progress, the theoretical understanding of diffusion distillation remains limited. In particular, it is still unclear how to quantify the error incurred when a teacher’s long-horizon transport is replaced by only a small number of learned maps, and how these errors accumulate under composition. A theoretical viewpoint is therefore useful for clarifying the limitations of few-step students and for guiding principled algorithm and time-grid design. We first quantify the network complexity required to approximate the time-dependent score, or equivalently the probability-flow velocity, associated with the marginals { p t } t ∈ [ 0 , T ] \{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,T]} , and track how this complexity depends on the geometry of the mixture distribution. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 3 introduces the GMM–OU setting and derives closed-form formulas for the score, the Hessian, and the stability bound of the probability-flow ODE. Section 4 studies score approximation by ReLU–ReQU networks and quantifies how the required network complexity depends on the mixture parameters and the target accuracy. Section 5 uses the Jacobian-based stability bound to identify a Lipschitz-mismatch obstruction for one-step distillation, proves an efficient approximation result for finite-time flow maps by deep residual compositions, and develops a stability-balanced time discretization rule. Section 6 provides empirical validation, and the appendices contain proofs and supporting technical results. 2 Related Work Theoretical studies of diffusion models. One line of theory studies diffusion models under general distributional assumptions and establishes approximation, statistical, and computational guarantees. Approximation results show that deep networks can approximate score functions while avoiding the curse of dimensionality under suitable structural assumptions [ 9 , 35 , 43 , 48 ] . Statistical analyses further show that the sample complexity can depend on the intrinsic dimension of the data distribution rather than the ambient dimension [ 4 , 5 , 26 ] . Other works connect score matching with neural tangent kernels to obtain generalization bounds [ 21 ] , or provide evaluation-complexity guarantees for higher-order training-free sampling schemes [ 28 ] . A second line of work studies diffusion models in analytically tractable regimes, with Gaussian mixtures serving as a canonical model class for deriving sharper guarantees. In this setting, prior work has studied parameter identifiability and recovery [ 17 , 38 ] , solver robustness [ 24 , 30 , 20 ] , and mechanisms for exact inversion or polynomial approximation [ 53 , 47 ] . The same mixture framework has also been used to characterize distributional dynamics and sampling limits, including critical windows for feature emergence [ 29 ] , sample-complexity estimates [ 8 ] , and discretization bounds [ 46 ] . It has further enabled analyses of training objectives, including limitations of guidance [ 7 ] , memorization trade-offs [ 3 , 15 , 57 ] , and velocity field matching [ 45 ] . These works provide important insights into diffusion dynamics, but they do not quantify the composition error that arises when a continuous-time flow is replaced by a short sequence of learned maps, which is the central operation in trajectory distillation. Our work belongs to this analytic line, but focuses on the missing composition mechanism. We formulate distillation as flow map approximation under composition and derive bounds that separate segment-level approximation error from dynamical amplification. To quantify this amplification, we specialize to an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process initialized from a Gaussian mixture. This setting remains nontrivial: although the forward dynamics are linear, the multimodal initialization induces a nonlinear score field in which posterior mixture weights can change rapidly, capturing the stiffness and perturbation sensitivity of the probability flow in low-noise regimes. By deriving closed-form expressions for the score and its Jacobian, we obtain computable bounds on the time-dependent Jacobian of the probability-flow ODE. This analysis explains why few-step students may fail in stiff multimodal regimes even when the score is accurately approximated at fixed times, and it motivates stability-balanced discretization rules that refine the time grid where error amplification is strongest. Stability, stiffness, and Lipschitz constraints. A related line of work studies stability and smoothness properties of diffusion dynamics, since stiff vector fields and large Lipschitz constants can hinder both training and sampling [ 54 , 50 ] . This regularity viewpoint has led to end-time scaling and Lipschitz-guided schedule design for mitigating singular behavior and mode collapse near the origin [ 50 , 6 ] . Within Gaussian mixture settings, researchers have also derived component-independent Lipschitz bounds and designed moment-matching solvers with rigorous sampling stability guarantees [ 30 , 20 ] . Our theory connects this stability viewpoint directly to multistage distillation. We show that the difficulty of a flow segment is determined not only by fixed-time score approximation, but also by the stiffness of the induced flow and its sensitivity to perturbations. This reveals regimes in which the score field is comparatively easy to approximate while the composed transport remains highly unstable. Based on the resulting time-dependent Jacobian bound, we derive a stability-balanced discretization rule that refines the time grid where amplification is large, thereby reducing error accumulation in stiff regimes. 3 Theoretical Setup This section follows the modeling framework of [ 9 ] and provides the technical setup for the later analysis.
